Mechanistic crosstalk between microglia and astrocytes in major depressive disorder (MDD)

Mechanistic crosstalk between microglia and astrocytes in major depressive disorder (MDD). The figure illustrates the mechanistic interactions between microglia and astrocytes under pathological conditions associated with MDD. Quiescent microglia become activated in response to pathogen‐associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), damage‐associated molecular patterns (DAMPs), and psychosocial stress via pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), Toll‐like receptors (TLRs), and the NOD‐like receptor thermal protein domain‐associated protein (NLRP3) inflammasome pathway. Upon activation, microglia adopt a pro‐inflammatory phenotype and release cytokines such as tumor necrosis factor‐alpha (TNF‐α), interleukin‐1 beta (IL‐1β), IL‐6, and IL‐18, as well as adenosine triphosphate (ATP) and complement proteins (C1q, C3). Astrocytes, initially exhibiting a neuroprotective A2 phenotype, respond to these inflammatory signals and convert to a neurotoxic A1 phenotype. A1 astrocytes are characterized by increased expression of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), excessive secretion of glutamate and d‐serine, exacerbating excitotoxic stress in microglia, and the release of ATP and lactate. Lactate induces metabolic activation of quiescent microglia and contributes to histone lactylation, an epigenetic modification that sustains the A1 reactive state. Furthermore, A1 astrocytes secrete pro‐inflammatory cytokines (TNF‐α, IL‐1β, IL‐6, interferon‐gamma [IFN‐γ]), amplifying immune responses and facilitating recruitment of peripheral immune cells, such as monocytes and T cells. Astrocyte‐derived ATP also drive calcium signaling cascades that activates purinergic P2X7 receptors on microglia, further enhancing microglial inflammatory activation. This reciprocal signaling establishes a positive feedback loop between microglia and astrocytes, perpetuating neuroinflammation and neuronal stress. In contrast, A2 astrocytes, which are associated with regenerative processes such as neurogenesis and tissue repair are functionally suppressed under MDD‐associated conditions. The cumulative outcome of this glial interplay includes chronic neuroinflammation, impaired neuroplasticity, synaptic loss, and the emergence of mood and cognitive symptoms characteristic of MDD
